claims.text: The study material is near-equiatomic, Co-free, solidified FeNiCrMn.
Partial-dislocation slip and cross-slip are the dominant plasticity mechanisms in dynamically loaded FeNiCrMn.
Partial-dislocation slip and cross-slip sustain strain hardening and ductility while preserving strength.
Fault or twin formation may contribute to the dynamic plasticity of FeNiCrMn.
The proposed starting material has a uniform grain-size distribution and low initial dislocation density.
The controlled study spans strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 and temperatures from -196 °C to 800 °C.
Dislocation configurations, stacking-fault density, and twin-boundary density evolve with strain rate and temperature.
FeNiCrMn has a moderate stacking-fault energy that facilitates partial-dislocation activity and cross-slip.
Dislocation-mediated deformation enhances strain hardening and delays plastic instability under quasi-static and high-rate loading.
Elevated temperature promotes dislocation climb and recovery in FeNiCrMn.
Dynamic flow stress is governed by competition among slip, partial-dislocation cross-slip, twinning, and thermally activated processes.
FeNiCrMn will show increased strain-rate sensitivity.
FeNiCrMn will maintain high strength and ductility throughout the tested temperature range.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates will produce dense dislocation networks and measurable stacking-fault or twinning features.
Elevated-temperature deformation will produce localized recovery.
Crystal-plasticity simulations will predict short-range order and partial-dislocation activity during dynamic deformation.
Prior dynamic studies of Co-containing and related high-entropy alloys found strain-rate-sensitive mechanical responses.
Extreme grain sizes, major compositional changes, or regimes outside the stated temperature and strain-rate ranges may activate brittle phases or dominant twinning.
The balance between twinning and partial-dislocation slip can shift with alloy purity or microstructure.
Observation of strength–ductility retention without increased partial-dislocation or cross-slip activity, or observation of a dominant alternative mechanism, would falsify the hypothesis.
